Once this first meaning is refuted, the other two cases are eliminated accordingly.
Question:

Since the provisional (upāya) and the ultimate (bhūtārtha) can serve as gates for one another, may the provisional also serve as the gate of the provisional, and the true aspect (lakṣaṇa) as the gate of the true aspect?

There are four propositions here; two are as previously explained. Third, the true nature (*dharmatā*) serves as the gateway to the true nature; fourth, skillful means (*upāya*) serves as the gateway to skillful means.

Just as a name is the gateway to its meaning and meaning is the gateway to its name—whereby the meaning of skillful means is manifested through the name of skillful means, thus the name is the gateway to the meaning—and whereby the meaning of skillful means corresponds to the name of skillful means, thus meaning is the gateway to the name—the true nature is likewise so.
As stated in the *Introduction to the Madhyamaka-śāstra*: "The reality is not realized apart from names; therefore, it is proclaimed by relying on the 'Middle. This is precisely what is meant.
Question:
Can three be manifested by means of three, and one by means of one?

This also consists of four propositions; two are as before. Regarding "manifesting three by means of three," it is said that the former three are different from the present one, such that these three exist outside of this one, and the present one is different from the former three, such that this one exists outside of those three. Therefore, the one is not the three-ones, and the three are not the one-three; all such views are merely attachments.

In order to cure this illness, I have differentiated and taught the One Buddha Vehicle as three; thus, the three are one, and the one is three. What you all practice is the Bodhisattva path; therefore, the one is three, and the three are one.

Since the three and the one are not mutually distinct, the principle of causes and conditions uses the three and the one of causes and conditions to manifest the three and the one of self-nature, and likewise uses the three and the one of self-nature to manifest the three and the one of causes and conditions; therefore, it is said that "the three manifest the one, and the one manifests the three."

Some cite fifteen locations of the "Gateways of Clarification": two in the "Expedient Means" chapter, six in the "Parable" chapter, three in the "Resolute Belief" chapter, two in the "City of Illusion" chapter, one in the "Dharma Master" chapter, and one in the "Avalokiteśvara" chapter.
Regarding the second [aspect], "expedient means" (upāya), it is a gate of wisdom; provisional wisdom serves as the gate to ultimate wisdom. Master Sheng says:
"Verbal teachings serve as the gate; since verbal teachings expound ultimate wisdom, verbal teachings are the gate to ultimate wisdom."
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fa-hua lun) is the same.
Next, it says that the Buddha-way is proclaimed through various dharma-gates; this takes the Mahāyāna teaching as the gate. There are six analogies for this:
first, the house is vast but has only a single gate, which likewise takes the Mahāyāna teaching as its gate.
2. "The gate that is being burned" refers to the three realms (*dhātu*) as the gate, just as one designates a house as a gate;
3. "There is only a single gate, and it is moreover narrow" refers to the Mahāyāna teaching as the gate;
4. "The three chariots are outside the gate" refers to the three realms as the gate.
Fifth, one exits the suffering of the triple world through the gates of the Buddha’s teachings; here, the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) serves as the gate.

Sixth, standing outside the gate, one relies on the Mahāyāna, using the boundaries of the two deaths as the gate; even those of the Small Vehicle who have exited beyond all afflictions (*kleśa*) and whose residual habits (*vāsanā*) are already exhausted are said to be "standing outside the gate."

In the "Chapter on Resolute Belief" (*Adhimukty-adhikāra*), there are three interpretations: first, that he stands by the side of the gate, where the principle and teaching of the Mahāyāna constitute the gate;
second, that he is still outside the gate, as described previously;
and third, that he is inside the gate of the elder, as described previously.

"Requesting the opening of the gate of ambrosia" refers both to the gates of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings; it also refers to the multiple gates and lofty pavilions, as well as the three gates of emptiness of the Hīnayāna.
The "gate of skillful means" (*upāya-mukha*) is explained as before.
The "Avalokiteśvara" [chapter] likewise takes the Great Teaching as its gate.
Now, regarding the explanation of "opening the gate of skillful means": that which was not previously taught is now all taught.
In the past, when all worldly affairs, livelihoods, and industries were taught, how could they have been considered skillful means?
Now, all of these are revealed as being non-contradictory with the true mark (*dharmatā*).

Formerly, the provisional means of the Hīnayāna and its fruits were taught; yet if even the fruits of the Hīnayāna are not the gate of the true reality (*dharmatā*), how much less could the minor expedients be such a gate?
Now all these are opened up as being the true reality itself. "What you practice is the Bodhisattva path"; this definitive resolution of the Śrāvaka teachings is the king of all sutras.
What was previously taught as the two gates of skillful means are now all revealed to be the true reality (dharmatā); how could they still be considered "gates"?

I cause all sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; in every form and every fragrance, there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma. Whether gate or non-gate, I open them all to reveal the true mark and manifest the water of the Buddha-nature.
If it were not opened, it would be deep, firm, obscure, and remote, such that no one could reach it; now that it is opened, one immediately perceives the water without any dry earth.
Furthermore, it may be explained through the three types of wisdom: all [other teachings] belong to this sutra, which constitutes the perfect *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing);
this sutra opens up the provisional means (*upāya*), which constitutes the perfect *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection).
"Revealing the true aspect" refers precisely to the perfect cultivation of wisdom.
These three [aspects] are profound and remote; now that the Buddha reveals them, one immediately attains the vision of reality.
The section beginning with "If there be a bodhisattva who hears... constitutes the fifth point: the exclusion of those who do not qualify.
If bodhisattvas hear this teaching and become startled or doubtful, or if śrāvakas harbor overweening pride, they are all like dry soil; they are not even moist soil, let alone having seen water.
From the passage beginning "If there be good men or good women after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa" onwards is the second section, which briefly indicates the method for propagating the sutra.
Furthermore, there are two parts:
first, showing the method; second, clarifying the benefits.
The method consists of three sections:
First, the presentation of the headings; second, the explanation; third, the exhortation to practice.
To dwell in the Tathāgata’s chamber is great compassion: if considered from the perspective of the same essence, it is the Dharma-body;
if it reaches out to sentient beings, it is liberation.
To enable sentient beings to realize their identity with the same essence (samatā) is precisely Prajñā.
Regarding the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s robe: if one considers that which is covered, it is the Dharmakāya;
if one considers that which covers and adorns the body, it is the patience of quiescent extinction (śānti-kṣānti).
If one considers the harmonizing with light to benefit all beings, it is liberation;
if one considers the act of sitting, it is prajñā;
if one considers that which is sat upon, it is the dharmakāya.
The body and seat being in profound resonance is itself liberation.

Furthermore, great compassion and peaceful bliss constitute the provision and accomplishment; gentleness, the subduing of anger, and the severance of delusions constitute the contemplative illumination; and sitting upon the seat constitutes the Dharma-body.

Within the "Peaceful Practices" (*Anrakugyō*), these three dharmas are further elaborated: the aforementioned "Adornments of the Tathāgata" refers to the robe; what was previously called "that which is borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata" refers to this seat; and the "carrying" (*tan*) refers to the act of carrying [the burden] into the chamber.
From the passage "In other lands" onwards is the second section, which encourages the circulation [of this sutra] by citing five benefits:

first, dispatching transformed persons; second, dispatching the fourfold assembly of transformed beings; third, dispatching the eight classes of supernatural beings; fourth, seeing the Buddha’s body; and fifth, bestowing the dhāraṇī.

If one's initial resolve is not yet pure, one may only dispatch emanated beings; one must not yet dispatch emanations of the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of supernatural beings. This is because if devas and nāgas were to see them, they might rely on this to become arrogant, thereby obstructing and harming their path; therefore, they should not be allowed to see them.
If the mind is free from attachment and reliance, one is capable of seeing the Buddha, let alone devas and nāgas, and let alone attaining the dhāraṇīs that bring self-realized benefit.
The verses consist of eighteen and a half lines and are divided into three parts:
first, one line that generally exhorts [the reader] not to repeat the prose;
second, sixteen and a half lines that versify the preceding prose.
The final line concludes with an exhortation.
Regarding the preceding section on praising [the teaching] by way of its fruit, there were five parts; here, first, one and a half lines of verse provide the opening analogy.

Next, "O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know," constitutes the second part, consisting of two and a half lines of verse that apply the analogy to the subject at hand (*yōjya*). It omits the remaining three parts—the proximate fruit, the explanation, and the exclusion of what is not [the true teaching].
In the section on the "Correct Path" (*fang gui*) within the preceding "General Exposition of the Sūtra," there are two parts:
the Correct Path and the Benefits.

Now, regarding these twelve and a half verses, the first three and a half verses praise the Correct Path; since that section contained three points, the present passage likewise praises those three meanings.
From "I [have benefited] thousands of millions of billions" onwards, the next nine lines praise the benefits.

The first line generally clarifies the Tathāgata’s intention to benefit through five matters; it is precisely because the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) pervades the ten directions that he is able to perform these five acts to protect practitioners.
The one and a half lines beginning with "If after my parinirvāṇa" praise the second [section], the dispatching of the fourfold assembly.
The one and a half lines beginning with "To guide" praise the first [section], the dispatching of the emanated person.
The two lines beginning with "If there is a person who preaches the Dharma" praise the fifth [benefit], enabling the attainment of *dhāraṇī*.
The line beginning with "If a person possesses these virtues" praises the fourth [benefit], enabling the vision of the Buddha.
The two lines beginning with “If a person is in a secluded place” [refer to] the third [section], which dispatches the eight classes of spirits, and so forth.
